Dakota (instead called Lakota by speakers of that dialect ) is the indigenous language of the Oc̣eṭi Ṡakowiƞ (Seven Council Fires) people of North America, consisting of the Bdewaḳaƞṭuƞwaƞ, Waḣpeḳute, Waḣpeṭuƞwaƞ, Sisiṭuƞwaƞ, Ihaƞkṭuƞwaƞ, Ihaƞkṭuƞwaƞna and Ṭiṭuƞwaƞ communities. Most members of these communities will describe themselves as Dakota (or Lakota for the Ṭiṭuƞwaƞ) people. Dakota and Lakota communities can be found in Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Montana, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. All of these places have a rich geography of names devised by Oc̣eṭi Ṡakowiƞ people in the Dakota/Lakota language, including rivers, lakes, towns, islands, hills and more. People have traveled since the dawn of human history and some areas once had Dakota/Lakota communities that presently do not, and so other areas (such as Wisconsin, Iowa, Wyoming and Ontario) also have locations with names in the language. Historically, there have been far, far more Dakota and Lakota place names than those that survive for us to learn about them in the present. Colonization has inflicted enormous trauma and language loss on these and other Native communities through allegedly-voluntary but actually forced exile from their lands, wars of conquest , traumatic boarding school assimilation, and more. When assigning Dakota and Lakota names to map elements, I am mainly drawing on the (often lifelong) work of others; very few of my changes are based on personal local knowledge. I have focused on sources who are either directly part of, or at least worked closely with, authentic Oc̣eti Ṡakowiƞ communities. This is the language of nations that are alive today, and they have things to say! My major sources include: My mapping work owes an enormous amount to (and sits in the shadow of) the absolutely incredible Maḳoc̣e Waṡte map by Lakota historian Dakota Wind Goodhouse, who drew on a vast range of sources to populate the names of thousands of places. His blog The First Scout is one of the best public history projects you’ll find anywhere, and you should check it out. Sometimes my research has led me to different conclusions on the precise meaning and pronunciation of some place names, and the largest limitation of his map is the one he tells you about right away (it is a Landscape Map and so rarely discusses towns and cities) but this is still the single largest, most thorough map of Lakota/Dakota place names you will find anywhere until such time as I can somehow map twice as much content as I have. Last updated on 17 November 2026. My mapping on OpenStreetMap includes names in both Dakota and Lakota, with ISO codes dak and lkt respectively. This is an unusual approach compared to a lot of other multilingual mapping, so it’s worth explaining in more detail. Dakota and Lakota are two different dialects of the same language (and are two possible names for that language). They are mutually intelligible, and a fluent speaker of one can understand a fluent speaker of the other without difficulty. An analogy might be made to the Spanish spoken in Mexico vs the Spanish spoken in Spain - a speaker of the other dialect will seem to have a strong accent, unusual pronunciation, and some different word choices, but they are still clearly speaking your language . Both dialects are endangered, but there are substantially more Lakota speakers than Dakota speakers and this has been true for a long time. Dakota and Lakota share the vast majority of their vocabulary. Most words that differ between these dialects differ in predictable, formulaic ways that do not represent any difference in meaning (e.g. Oṭuƞwe vs Otȟúŋwahe or Bde vs Ble). The most meaningful differences in Lakota vs Dakota speech emerge in conversational flow, which rarely matters for place names. Close Tuwewanzi's Diary Dakota/Lakota Writing Systems and Orthography Posted by Tuwewanzi on 12 November 2026 in English . The Dakota/Lakota language has been a written language for only the most recent chapters of its history. Writing systems for the language were first devised by 19th-century missionaries who sought to promote literacy as a part of encouraging Dakota people to convert to Christianity. These missionaries, especially Stephen Riggs , developed an alphabet based on the Latin Alphabet to represent the sounds present in the language. All widely used methods for writing the language today are based on Riggs’ system with some degree of variation. There is no single writing system accepted by the vast majority of speaker communities. A variety of systems - or orthographies - exist with varying degrees of popularity, and invididual speakers and teachers often have strong preferences one way or another. Areas of debate include: May an orthography make use of special characters (ŋ, ǧ, ḳ, ú) or should writing be done only with characters that can be written with a standard English keyboard? The language contains vowels (a, i, u) that may be nasalized or not, depending on context; should the orthography note the difference? The language contains consonants (z, c, p, t, k, s) that may be aspirated for a harder sound or unaspirated; should the orthography note the difference? pages.description: Long thought to have been looted from northern England by Scottish tribes, the larger-than-life leg may have actually been displayed in Roman Scotland, before it was carefully dismantled and buried by retreating forces
pages.text: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged to a Towering Statue of a Roman Emperor on Horseback Skip to main content Curator Fraser Hunter examines the bronze leg. Duncan McGlynn In 1820, a larger-than-life gilded bronze lower leg was pulled out of a bog in the Scottish Borders region. For more than two centuries, historians discredited the idea that the Roman-era artifact came from Scotland, instead assuming that it was hacked off a monument in England and hauled north by marauding tribes. But ahead of “ Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire ,” an exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland (NMS), researchers have determined that the so-called “Milsington leg” was not stolen from the south, nor was it violently severed. Instead, they posit that it formed part of a colossal equestrian statue of the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius that once stood in southern Scotland in the second century C.E., before it was dismantled by retreating Roman troops. “This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland,” Fraser Hunter , principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at NMS, says in a statement . The bronze leg shows no signs of being violently hacked off the larger statue. The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent. The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries. French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families. Have a diabetes management plan, ideally before, during, and after pregnancy, to keep you and your baby healthy. Before you get pregnant Manage your blood sugar Many doctors recommend that you reach and stay at your A1C goal for a few months before becoming pregnant. People with type 1 diabetes need to take insulin every day. Currently, type 1 diabetes can't be prevented, but it can be treated effectively. What is type 1 diabetes? If you have type 1 diabetes, your pancreas doesn't make insulin or makes very little insulin. Insulin helps blood sugar enter the cells in your body for use as energy. Without insulin, blood sugar can't get into cells and builds up in the bloodstream. High blood sugar is damaging to the body and causes many of the symptoms and complications of diabetes. Type 1 diabetes is less common than type 2 —about 5-10% of people with diabetes have type 1. Learn more about this connection and how to care for your liver. All about your liver Your liver is the largest internal organ in your body, and it's responsible for many vital functions, including: Filtering your blood to remove wastes like chemicals or toxins. Breaking down medicines and other substances. Producing bile, which helps you digest fat. Helping your immune system fight germs that could make you sick. Your liver also plays a key role in balancing your blood sugar levels. When you eat, a hormone called insulin removes extra sugar from your bloodstream. This sugar is stored in your liver for future use. Between meals and overnight, your liver releases that sugar back into your bloodstream so your body has the energy it needs. May 15, 2024 Español Types of Insulin Key points Many types of insulin are used to treat diabetes. Insulin is classified by how fast and how long it works in your body. pages.description: Australian Jai Opetaia withdraws from his heavyweight fight with Deontay Wilder on the undercard of Tyson Fury's bout with Anthony Joshua in December.
pages.text: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua: Jai Opetaia pulls out of Deontay Wilder fight - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Deontay Wilder (left) has won 45 of his 50 fights, while Jai Opetaia has never lost By Kal Sajad BBC Sport boxing journalist Published 18 November 2026 Australian Jai Opetaia has withdrawn from his heavyweight fight with Deontay Wilder on the undercard of Tyson Fury's bout with Anthony Joshua. Unbeaten cruiserweight champion Jai Opetaia was set to step up to heavyweight for the first time to face American Wilder at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December. Opetaia, 31, did not give a reason for his withdrawal, but it is understood he aggravated a hand injury in training. "Apologies to everyone and especially [Wilder] and his team for withdrawing from the bout," he wrote on Instagram. "Fighter to fighter, I know the feeling and it's frustrating. I've always prided myself on fighting anyone, any place." Opetaia criticised "keyboard warriors" who suggested he was scared off by Wilder's powerful right hand. Opetaia, who has won all 31 of his professional bouts, reiterated his ambition to become undisputed cruiserweight champion. Unified champion David Benavidez has expressed an interest in facing Opetaia in 2027. Britons queuing up to fight Wilder Opetaia's withdrawal leaves a significant gap on the undercard of one of the biggest all-British heavyweight fights in history. It remains unclear whether former world champion Wilder, 41, will still feature on the bill, but several British heavyweights have expressed an interest in replacing Opetaia.

pages.text: U.K. singer-songwriter Arlo Parks on touring and her greatest travel adventures | National Geographic TRAVEL U.K. singer-songwriter Arlo Parks on touring and her greatest travel adventures The Mercury Prize-winning singer-songwriter talks dancing on the streets of São Paulo and finding creativity in the Cotswolds. Arlo Parks’s new album Ambiguous Desire is out in April via Transgressive Records. _sullman By Graeme Green Published April 9, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). What’s your earliest travel memory? Going to the south of France. My parents used to drive straight down from London to Nice, sometimes in one 17-hour road trip. We’d listen to my dad’s audiobooks and watch cartoons in the back. I remember spending time in different parts of the south, going through olive trees and to the ocean. I was at my bookworm peak, so I’d always go out to a field or tuck myself away in a corner of the house to read. Do you have a favourite place in the world? São Paulo in Brazil. I loved wandering the streets, getting lost, exploring street markets. I went dancing in clubs with these little local bands of 70-year-old men who’d been playing in jazz outfits since they were 20. They had everyone dancing in the streets, it was really special. I have Brazilian ancestry, so I felt like I was home in a way. Arlo Parks has Brazilian ancestry and feels right at home in São Paulo's buzzy streets. André Klotz Where is your favourite venue to play in? So far, The Greek Theatre in LA. pages.text: U.S. birth rate continues to fall : NPR Accessibility links Skip to main content Keyboard shortcuts for audio player U.S. birth rate continues to fall The U.S. fertility rate continued its slide to historic levels, due to plunging teen pregnancies and far more women delaying motherhood into their 30s and 40s. News 710,000 fewer babies were born last year in U.S. compared with two decades ago April 9, 2026 2:45 PM ET Brian Mann File photo showing babies in a U.S. maternity ward. The fertility rate in the U.S. has dropped steadily. Last year, there were roughly 710,000 fewer children born in the U.S. compared with the peak in 2007. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption toggle caption i Seth Wenig/AP Women in the U.S. gave birth to roughly 710,000 fewer children last year compared with the nation's peak in 2007, according to preliminary data released this week by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Lead researcher Brady Hamilton, a demographer with the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, said the latest one percent drop in "general fertility" from 2024 to 2025 is part of a long-running downward trend. "Since 2007, there's been a decline in the general fertility rate [in the U.S.] of 23%," Hamilton told NPR. The impact of that change in real numbers is sizable: In 2007, there were 4,316,233 babies born . Last year, even though the nation's population as a whole is larger, there were only 3,606,400 newborns . Our Mission Our History Our Statistical Programs Censuses Surveys Population Estimates and Projections Data Tools and Apps Research Geography International Stats Regional Offices U.S. Census Bureau at a Glance [<1.0 MB] Our Mission The Census Bureau's mission is to serve as the nation’s leading provider of quality data about its people and economy. We honor privacy, protect confidentiality, share our expertise globally, and conduct our work openly. We are guided on this mission by scientific objectivity, our strong and capable workforce, our devotion to research-based innovation, and our abiding commitment to our customers. Our History Thomas Jefferson directed the first census in 1790. As required by the U.S. Constitution, a census has been taken every 10 years thereafter. In 1840, the Census Act authorized the establishment of a centralized Census Office. In 1902, the Census Office became a permanent organization within the Department of the Interior. A year later, it was renamed the Bureau of the Census and moved to the new Department of Commerce and Labor. Search for information on your state, county, or city. What is the U.S. Census? The U.S. Census Bureau provides data about the nation’s people and economy. Every 10 years, it conducts a census counting every resident in the United States. The most recent census was in 2020. Who must participate? By law, all U.S. residents are required to take part in the census. To protect people’s privacy, all personal information collected by the census is confidential for 72 years. The policy represents a commitment to conducting rigorous, relevant evaluations and to using evidence from evaluations to inform policy and practice. DOL seeks to promote rigor, relevance, transparency, independence, and ethics in the conduct of evaluations. This policy addresses each of these principles. The mission of the Department of Labor is to "...foster, promote, and develop the welfare of the wage earners, job seekers, and retirees of the United States; improve working conditions; advance opportunities for profitable employment; and assure work-related benefits and rights." The importance of these goals demands that we continually innovate and improve, and that we evaluate the performance and effectiveness of our programs and activities. Through evaluation, DOL can learn systematically so that we can make our services as effective as possible. Evaluation produces one type of evidence. A learning organization with a culture of continual improvement requires many types of evidence, including not only evaluation but also descriptive research studies, performance measurement, financial and cost data, survey statistics, and program administrative data. U.S. Gridded Methane Emissions The gridded EPA U.S. methane greenhouse gas inventory (gridded methane GHGI) includes time series of annual methane emission maps with 0.1° x 0.1° (~ 10 x 10 km) spatial and monthly temporal resolution for the contiguous United States (CONUS). This gridded methane inventory is designed to be consistent with methane emissions from the U.S. EPA Inventory of U.S. Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Sinks (U.S. GHGI). The gridded methane GHGI dataset includes annual methane emission fluxes for over 25 inventory emission source categories, including those from agriculture, petroleum and natural gas systems, coal mining, and waste. Gridded methane emissions data are generated by allocating national annual U.S. GHGI methane emissions from individual source categories to a 0.1° x 0.1° CONUS grid, using a series of spatial and temporal 'proxy' datasets at the state, county, and grid levels. Where possible, proxy data are the same data used to develop the U.S. GHGI so that the gridded emissions can be, as closely as possible, a spatial and temporal representation of the national-level U.S. GHGI. Christmas day, 1918, was for many Americans their first experience of that season in a foreign land, thousands of miles from home, among people of different race, language, and sympathy. When we realize that over two million of our young men were in France at the time, it seems appropriate, on the approach of another Christmas, to recall that day—a day we shall remember as long as we live—our different Christmas. At that time active hostilities were over, of course, but many combat divisions still held their lines just where the fighting had ceased on November 11. The following account tells how the men of my organization, the 158th lnfantry Brigade, made the most of circumstances and celebrated their Christmas with a spirit of cheer and good-will that overcame all obstacles, even rising above the curse of Meuse rains, the amazing mud and slime of French battlefields. Credit: Burrows/JILA JILA researchers have designed a microscope instrument so stable that it can accurately measure the 3D movement of individual molecules over many hours—hundreds of times longer than the current limit measured in seconds. The technology was designed to track the machinery of biological cells, down to the tiniest bits of DNA, a single "base pair" of nucleotides among the 3 billion of these chemical units in human genes. But the instrument could be useful well beyond biology, biochemistry and biophysics, perhaps in manufacturing. Located 400 miles from Anchorage, Unalakleet has approximately 800 residents and is accessible only by plane. At its headwaters, the Unalakleet River is swift and channelized; once it reaches the valley floor it begins to meander. For most of its length, the river has a varying pool/riffle nature, which offers a diversity of boating and fishing opportunities. The upper 81 miles of the Unalakleet River are designated a National Wild River. A designated wild river is free of impoundments and generally inaccessible except by trail, with primitive shorelines and unpolluted waters. The BLM manages the Unalakleet National Wild River to provide high-quality primitive recreation opportunities, protect water quality, protect historic and archaeological values, and preserve the remarkable fisheries resources for which the river was designated. pages.text: Uncover Remote Trails on These U.K. Request Stop Hikes | National Geographic By Billy Thomas Published October 23, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The UK is renowned for its rural hikes — the kind of walks that lead you over mossy stiles and through creaking kissing gates. Walks that would be perfect were it not for the fact that many are hard to reach by road. There is, of course, another way: rail-to-trail hiking, which involves catching a train to your hiking destination, via a request stop. Across Britain, there are more than 100 stations that scheduled trains won’t call at unless requested on board or from the platform. Often remote and far from busy motorways or bustling cities, these stops offer the ideal way to get off the beaten track. Check out our favourites below — all offering breathtaking views and hidden history. Duncraig Castle is on the shores of Loch Carron — a sea loch that connects to the Inner Sound. Learn how to claim your refund if you did not file a return or if your check never got to you. Undelivered federal tax refunds If you never received your tax refund To replace a lost or stolen tax refund check, you can request a refund trace in the IRS Where’s My Refund tool . You will need to enter your Social Security number, filing status, and the exact whole dollar amount of your refund. The IRS uses refund traces to track lost or stolen checks or verify whether a check was deposited. Find out how to request a refund trace and replace your refund check. If you cannot get your refund status after checking online You can also call the IRS to check on the status of your refund. Wait times to speak with a representative can be long. But you can avoid waiting by using the automated phone system. Follow the message prompts when you call. If you moved after filing your return Refund checks are mailed to your last known address. If you move without notifying the IRS or the U.S. Postal Service (USPS), your refund check may be returned to the IRS. Submit a Change of Address Form 8822 [PDF, 81KB] to the IRS.
